label: Title
notes: Open with the central change in viewpoint. Earlier chapters can discuss length abstractly; this chapter explains how a smooth manifold manufactures length from tangent data and then asks which global metric statements survive. Keep the source grounding visible: Chapter 5, printed pages 135-208, PDF pages 150-223.

label: Six Mechanisms
notes: Use the six mechanisms as a map, not as a list. The same sentence should keep returning: choose admissible tangent vectors, assign an infinitesimal cost, integrate along curves, and then extract metric consequences. This prepares students to compare Riemannian, hyperbolic, sub-Riemannian, and Finsler behavior.

label: Riemannian Length
notes: Make the definition operational. A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying inner product, and the length of a curve is the integral of its instantaneous norm. Stress that the distance is not specified directly; it is recovered by minimizing lengths of connecting curves.

label: Metric Tensor Figure
notes: Read the figure from left to right. Ellipses show how tangent vectors are priced at different base points, and the sampled curve accumulates cost through that field. The positive-definite badge is important because without it the integral can stop behaving like length.

label: Worked Length
notes: Treat this as a concrete calculation rather than a theorem slide. The same parametrized curve has Euclidean length about 3.545 and Riemannian length about 4.034 in the sampled metric, so the metric tensor increases the travel cost by about 13.8 percent.

label: Exponential Map
notes: Introduce the exponential map as the geodesic launcher. A vector at p records initial direction and speed; following the geodesic for unit time lands on the manifold. The point is local coordinate production, not global one-to-one behavior.

label: Gauss Lemma
notes: Use Gauss lemma as the geometric reason normal coordinates are so useful. Radial geodesics meet geodesic spheres orthogonally, so first-order distance from p is readable as radius. The numerical residual is essentially zero in the sphere model.

label: Poincare Warning
notes: The Poincare disk is a warning against trusting Euclidean appearance. The boundary is infinitely far away in the hyperbolic metric, geodesics are boundary-orthogonal arcs, and angles are Euclidean-looking because the model is conformal. Ask students to separate three ideas that the drawing overlays: topology of an open disk, Euclidean screen coordinates, and the hyperbolic length element.

label: Hyperbolic Lab
notes: Frame the lab as an inspection tool. Students should look for two features: geodesics as boundary-orthogonal circles or diameters, and horocycles tangent to the ideal boundary. The isometry badge says the sampled disk transformation preserved hyperbolic distance up to floating-point error.

label: Sub-Riemannian Directions
notes: Sub-Riemannian geometry changes the admissible directions rather than merely changing their weights. Curves must stay horizontal, so the metric is defined through constrained controls. This makes reachability a bracket question. Emphasize that forbidden instantaneous motion may still be produced indirectly by short loops, which is why local geometry becomes anisotropic at different scales.

label: Ball Box
notes: Explain the commutator loop slowly: move along V, then W, then back along V, then back along W. In ordinary flat intuition this should close, but the noncommuting vector fields create vertical drift. The ball-box picture records the scaling: horizontal order r, bracket order r squared.

label: Volume Comparison
notes: Separate the two volume stories. Riemannian volume comes from the determinant of the metric tensor. Finsler volume needs a convention because the unit ball can be non-elliptic; Busemann and Holmes-Thompson encode different normalizations. Point out that both conventions agree on the Euclidean disk but respond differently to diamond and square tangent balls.

label: Finsler Table
notes: Use the table to make polar duality tangible. The l2 row normalizes both densities to one, while l1 and linf exchange large and small unit/polar balls. The moral is that a Finsler norm has both primal and dual geometry built into volume.

label: Besikovitch Inequality
notes: State Besikovitch as a lower-bound principle. If a cube-like region keeps opposite faces separated by prescribed distances, then its volume cannot collapse below the product scale. The model verifies a positive margin between area and the product bound.

label: Proof Roadmap
notes: The proof roadmap is the topological lock. Distance-to-face functions give nonexpanding coordinates, boundary behavior forces a degree-one map, and degree one forces coverage of the target box. Analysis then turns nonexpansion into a Jacobian bound.

label: Artifact Lab
notes: Run this as a short artifact-reading lab. Each group chooses one artifact, states what geometric object it encodes, reads one numeric badge, and names one possible misconception the artifact prevents. The aim is to connect computation, visualization, and theorem language.

label: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to reconstruct the chapter from one curve and one box. A curve tests tangent norms, geodesics, and admissibility; a box tests volume and face-distance lower bounds. The exit exercise asks them to decide what changes when the tangent norm stops being inner-product based.
